questions.question: Describe the pattern of volcanoes on a world map, naming the Ring of Fire and one other belt.
questions.expected_answer: Volcanoes are found in narrow belts along plate boundaries, not randomly. The Pacific Ring of Fire, about 40 000 km around the edges of the Pacific (New Zealand, Indonesia, Japan, Alaska, the west coasts of the Americas), has about three-quarters of active volcanoes. Other belts: the Mediterranean (Vesuvius, Etna), mid-ocean ridges such as Iceland, and the East African Rift (Kilimanjaro, Nyiragongo).

questions.question: Explain why volcanoes form at divergent boundaries, at subduction zones and at hot spots.
questions.expected_answer: Divergent: as plates move apart, pressure on the mantle drops and rock melts; magma rises into the gap. Subduction: a sinking oceanic plate releases water into the mantle above, lowering its melting point so magma forms and rises to form a chain of volcanoes. Hot spots: plumes of very hot mantle material rise beneath a plate, melting through it to form volcanoes such as Hawaii.

questions.question: Compare shield and composite volcanoes in terms of magma, eruption type and shape, with an example of each.
questions.expected_answer: Shield: runny, low-silica basalt magma lets gas escape; effusive eruptions with long lava flows; broad, gentle slopes; e.g. Mauna Loa. Composite: sticky, high-silica magma traps gas; explosive eruptions of ash, bombs and pyroclastic flows; steep cones of layered ash and lava; e.g. Mount Fuji, Vesuvius, Mount St Helens.
